reading.rtitle: Read the Figure Before the Text
paras: Ask an experienced researcher how they read a new paper and most of them will admit to the same habit. They read the title, they skip the introduction, and they go straight to the figures. Not because the text does not matter, but because the figures are where the data actually is. Everything else is somebody telling you what the data means, and it is worth knowing what you think before you hear what they think.

That only works if the figure can stand on its own, and that is the job of the caption. A good caption tells you what was measured, in what units, in which groups and over how long, so that a reader who never opens the text can still say what the figure shows. A weak caption says Figure 2: Results. It forces you back into the paragraphs to find out what the two lines are, and by then you are reading the authors' story instead of the numbers.

Reading a figure well is mostly a matter of order. Start with the axes: what is on each one, and where does the scale begin? A vertical axis that starts at forty instead of zero can turn a small rise into a dramatic one. Then look for the trend, the overall direction, before any single point. Then compare the groups. Only then look at the strange point that does not fit, because one outlier is easy to notice and very easy to overinterpret.

The last step is the one most students skip, and it is the reason this matters for your own writing. Describing a figure and explaining it are two different jobs. The results section says what happened: the treated group rose steadily and leveled off at about eighty percent, roughly twice the control. Why it happened belongs to the discussion. A sentence that does both at once is almost always claiming more than the figure can show.

listenings.text: Right, everybody, Figure 3, and before anybody says what it means, I want you to tell me what it shows. On the horizontal axis we have days, from zero to fourteen. On the vertical axis, the percentage of seeds that germinated. Two groups. The black line is the control, the green line is the seeds we soaked overnight. Look at the green line first. Almost nothing happens for three days, then it rises sharply between day three and day six, from about ten percent to about sixty. After that the rise slows down, and it levels off at roughly eighty-five percent by day ten. The control rises too, but steadily, without that jump, and it finishes at about forty. So by the end, the soaked group is roughly twice as high as the control. There is one strange point, day eight in the control, where it suddenly drops to twenty and then comes back. That is one tray, and I would not build an argument on it. Notice what I have not said. I have not said why the soaking works. That is a different conversation, and it comes after this one.

Hi, it is me again. I have finished the table for the results section and I want to read it to you before I send it, because I am not sure the numbers say what I think they say. So, three sites, and we counted the same species at each one in March and again in August. At the first site, the number fell slightly, from forty-two to thirty-eight, which is honestly almost nothing. At the second site, it fell sharply, from fifty-five to nineteen, so it lost roughly two thirds. And at the third site it actually rose, from twelve to thirty, which is more than double. My problem is the summary sentence. I had written that the population declined across all sites, and that is just not true, is it? Two out of three declined, and the decline at the first site is so small it might be noise. I think the honest sentence is that it fell sharply at one site, barely changed at another, and more than doubled at the third. Can you tell me if that sounds too complicated for a results section?
